utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That's not a problem. Twenty-six years ago, there was some slight sentence, not for robbery. But it was wiped out on the basis our law because they were small problems. I was only 19 years at the time, but it wasn't robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber for what offences you were convicted of.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, without going round the problem, I don't really remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I've got some other questions to ask you now. When did you start writing your book on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1999. Summer, autumn. Late summer, early autumn. Late summer, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Has the book been published or completed?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book is being completed. It is in the stage of completion. An interview was published and an article, an excerpt from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did the British security service contact you about your book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British intelligence service never contacted me in connection with the book but in connection with the discovery of Serb victims in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have the British security service paid you money as part of your funds for writing this book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It gave a sum which was supposed to cover about 50 per cent of the expenses of the research, because there was quite considerable research linked to the writing of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In what circumstances did it come about that the British security service were paying you funds for the expenses of this book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because one of the subjects in the book was research into Serb victims in Kosovo and sending in information about that, among others, to the International Tribunal in The Hague, and Milosevic and his men refused to do so, to supply that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you declare this interest of the British security service in your book to your political party or any other agency, government agency?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To which agencies?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The money that was paid to you, we were told, was 3.000 euros. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said approximately 5.000 euros in two instalments, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how was that money paid to you? Was it cash or to a bank account?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cash, with no records. I didn't have to mention it or bring it up here in this Tribunal. There is no bank account, nothing. It was in cash for 50 per cent of the expenses of the research, as the rest of the 50 per cent was supplied by -- was supplied by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you had businesses and that you were successful in business. Why did you need the money from the British security service of 5.000 euros?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a businessman. I am a manufacturer of goods, a producer of goods, a small scale industrialist and for nine years I spent my own money in politics, but due to the costs of the war and the different problems that arose with regard to myself and my family, I was not able to finance all my activities and that is why I asked for assistance as this was of general national interest. And I reported this to the State Security Service of Serbia, so there was no secret on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did the State Security Service of Serbia give their approval of your writing this book with the aid of money from the British security service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. They even started collecting documents and information about the Serb victims. And this was dispersed in different boxes and trucks, this information, or storehouses, rather, warehouses, not trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us last week that the book concerned the victims of Kosovo. Was that victims exclusively who were Serb or also Albanian victims?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic thesis of the book is that Mr. Milosevic caused a war in which both the Albanians and the Serbs fell victim. In view of the fact that the Albanians victims are already common knowledge, more or less, the book starts out from the premises of Serb victims but of course just as part of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did the British security service tell you what interest they had in you writing and publishing this book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Their interest was twofold: One was to secure via unofficial channels some facts on Serb victims which Mr. Milosevic did not supply at the time; and the second interest was that we have a well-balanced out picture of what actually did happen in 1998 and 1999 in that unfortunate circumstance that befell all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ask them for money or did they suggest that they would pay you money?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked them, because I said that I would not be able to finance the costs and expenditure of the research and that, if they were willing, they could meet 50 per cent of the expenses in view of the fact that I knew them for a long time and that it was a subject that was of common interest. So I contacted them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you say, would that subject be that it was anti or against Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The British side, like myself, was interested in seeing a realistic, or as close to real as possible, of the image of what was going on in Kosovo. No mention was made of any specific interest against Milosevic because The Hague indictment had already been raised against him. Therefore, it was quite clear that there were other -- that there was other evidence except for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you say, then, that it was accepted by both of you that the book would be anti-Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book was to be the truth or as close to the truth as possible. Whether that was anti-Milosevic or not, that's another matter. The book did not deal in anti-Milosevic positions but in ascertaining as correctly as possible the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have any other security services paid you any money?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not until I left the country. Only once I had left the country, but that was a private affair altogether at that point in time. And not money. It wasn't money. When I left the country, it wasn't a question of money, it was assistance with regard to accommodation for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in need of money to support yourself when you left Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a brief period of time, yes, because I had to leave Serbia in a great hurry, and lots -- I did not manage to have all the debts owed me paid in. So 150.000 euros, claims to that effect, claims that were not paid to me to that amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you avoid the payment of bills yourself when you left Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite simply, I had no accounts abroad. So there was no one to pay in except the firm's accounts. But of course, private affairs and the affairs of the firm cannot be mixed up. And my firm, my company, was frozen for two years anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you settle all the outstanding accounts and bills owing by you at the time that you had left Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the money I was to have been repaid was ten times greater than the bills that I had to be paid. So before I got the money paid to me, I wasn't able to settle my outstanding accounts and bills. But nobody is persecuting me for that, because the bills I should have paid are far smaller than my claims. So nobody's after me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Since leaving Yugoslavia, you've said that you had some slight assistance from another security service while you established yourself in accommodation, I just want to ask you some questions now about your circumstances without you giving any personal details in public. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I don't understand what you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you been provided with a new country in which to live?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not up until now. Whether I shall be or not, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you're currently seeking asylum in another country. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to see about that with the OTP office of The Hague Tribunal. I have not officially asked for asylum because I can live in a third country even without the asylum status. But perhaps I will ask for it. I really didn't deal with the question of my future in any great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But is the position that you will be given a new identity in another country? I don't want the details, but just whether that fact is true or not.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely untrue. A new identity abroad. I never discussed that with anybody, nor would I accept it. I have no reason to ask for a new identity. Protection is one matter, a new identity is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Did you wish me to deal with the questions posed to me by Judge Kwon before I re-examine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whichever is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I may do that, and the third of those questions may well lead into my re-examination, if I may. In the first place, Your Honour, my -- according to my note, Your Honour asked about a document, 147.3, and referred to the fact that in the document dated the 31st of, I believe it's July 1997, there appeared to be references in Cyrillic script to this particular witness which do not appear on the English translation that was provided. My understanding is that the copy that was sent for translation at that particular time was sent in a redacted form with the name, of course, because this was a protected witness, with the name -- that then was a protected witness, the name redacted. Therefore, the translation that has been submitted under 147.3 does not contain the witness's name and the translation is written in such a way as to try to make sense of it without the name in it. My understanding is that we have requested a subsequent translation of this document in its unredacted form, and that is forthcoming. If it would assist, we could place the unredacted document on the ELMO now and perhaps have the translators or the interpreters read a couple of aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did Your Honour respond that you'd like to put it on the ELMO now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Other translations indicate that there are some parts redacted but this does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct. It's two pages but the first page is being placed on the ELMO now. And I suspect that it's the underlined aspects that were in fact redacted when it was sent for translation. So if the interpreters are able to read this particular exhibit as it's now displayed, perhaps we could go to, first of all, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but somebody from the courtroom will have to read the text first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm unable, of course, to read the Cyrillic text, so I'm unable to assist in that regard. Perhaps that could be shown to the witness who, I take it, can read it, and perhaps the witness will be prepared to read that for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, Witness, I'm go to ask you, if you would please, underneath the headline, there appears to be a reference. Could you read the caption, if you would, please, in Cyrillic, out loud so the translator can interpret.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subtitle is: "The previous authority led by Salih Denicoc [phoen], the Social Democrats of Albania have not been hit by the virus of nationalism, says Predrag Simic. The Social Democrats and Democratic Alliance of Albania are turned towards European integrations and tendencies of the new European left, is the opinion of Ratomir Tanic. After this signal from Tirana, the politicians of the Albanian parties in Kosovo are starting to reassess their positions." That is the subtitle. Do you wish me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to the column where it is underlined and read the underlined sentence in its entirety, please. That was the three columns, the three vertical columns, the left one appears to have a sentence underlined. Could you read that to us.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the whole sentence is a lengthy one, and it says: "As to what the relationships were like between the SRY and Serbia with neighbouring Albania and their possible improvement after the mentioned statement as well as the repercussions on the viewpoints of the leaders of political parties of Albanians in Kosmet, we talked to Dr. Predrag Simic, the director of Institute for International Politics and Economics, and Ratomir Tanic, advisor for international relations in the Novo Demokratija party, with experts who took part in the negotiations for a solution to the Serbian-Albanian problem in Kosmet, Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the remaining highlights, you will see a name underlined. Is that your name, in fact, that's been underlined?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours wish me to have the entire article written, I understand that the translation is available tomorrow. Thank you. That deals with that. Now, the second document that Your Honours have asked for clarification was the document 148, which was marked, I believe, as an attachment to this witness's statement as item TX-5, and TX-5 was noted in the statement to be missing a page, as it were, and in fact, TX-6 in the statement was a document which included the first five pages in TX-5 and the additional pages -- the balance of page 5 and a final page as well. That has not been marked as an exhibit. I would ask to substitute TX-6, which we have copies of here, for item TX-5. So if this could have a new exhibit number. This is the entire article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the front page, there are some parts redacted. What are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I'm afraid I -- the original, I believe, that has been given to the registrar and marked as an exhibit is in its unredacted form, but I have a redacted copy as well, Your Honour. But I believe the original that has been marked as an exhibit is in unredacted form. 148.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked 148A.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I propose now, in re-examination, to deal with the third issue that Your Honour has mentioned, but if I may, I propose to ask a few questions about it in the course of re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, during your cross-examination, you have been challenged about -- that you were never in a position to know many of the matters to which you have testified to. In response, among other things, you've said that you've testified only about those matters which there is independent corroboration for what you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I did not present my overall knowledge because I cannot corroborate my overall knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, sir, in particular dealing with conversations which you refer to both in your evidence and in your statement that you had with Momcilo Perisic while you were preparing your book, I believe you indicated that he showed you a letter dated the spring of 1998 that he apparently sent to the accused Milosevic while Mr. Perisic was still the Chief of Staff of the VJ, and that's at page 19 of your statement. Do you recall testifying to that matter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in that letter, it's alleged that Mr. Perisic pointed out some six points he referred to as negative facts, and in so doing, in effect complaining that Mr. Milosevic was cutting Mr. Perisic out of the chain of command of the VJ. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I understand that the book itself has not been marked as an exhibit. I have a copy of it here, and I understand the accused was provided with a copy, or borrowed the copy - I don't know if that's been returned - but an extract of page 160, I believe, was entered as Exhibit 150. Now, I just want to ask some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I'm showing you -- if you could look at me, I'm showing you a book which is authored by Messrs. Dejan Lukic and Pero Simic, and its translated title is "Fire and Flood." Are you familiar with that book?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw that book for the first time three or four days ago, when I was provided with a photocopy of Perisic's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the usher assist. I'm just going to show this page, the inside page, which indicates its publication date, please. Could you show that could the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There appears -- I'm showing you a single page of that book, which appears to have the names of the two authors at the top, a title in the middle, and then an address and date as to publication. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title page of the book, Filip Visnjic is a publishing house in Belgrade, 2001. Pero Simic and Dejan Lukic are the authors of the book "Fire and Food," which is the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And perhaps I might -- I don't know whether it's gone in as part of the exhibit or not, but I have a copy of that title page. Was it marked originally as part of Exhibit 150? Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could -- sorry. I'm going to turn to page 160 that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At page 160 of that book, labelled Appendix 2, you will find a letter dated the 23rd of July 1998 from Momcilo Perisic, addressed to then-President Slobodan Milosevic of the FRY. Is that the letter to which you referred in your evidence? Is that the letter that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I know that because it wasn't just the letter that was shown to me but Mr. Perisic and I had a long discussion about the contents of that letter. So the letter wasn't just shown to me but it was the subject of a lengthy discussion between me and Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, this letter is dated the 28th of July, 1998, according to its publication date as Appendix 2 to that book. When, approximately, did you first see the letter when you discussed it with Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of the existence of the letter earlier than that, but I saw the letter itself for the first time in the summer of 1999. But I knew that the letter existed immediately after it had been written. But I didn't see it then, I saw it in the summer of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, is it true, sir, that you gave your statement to officials of the ICTY over the course of several interviews between the 21st of June, 1999, and the 19th of July, 2000?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And we've already seen that, according to the publication date, that letter was not published until 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, secondly, sir, in your statement, I believe in the course -- in the English version, pages 30 to 32, and in your evidence, you refer to conveying information to the accused Milosevic about two secret offers of settlement, both just before the bombing commenced and after it had started, and the purpose of that was to indicate that it was possible to negotiate peacefully with the West. You also refer to Zoran Lilic's involvement, in your statement. Would you look at page 166 of that same book. That's Appendix 4. Do you recognise the document at Appendix 4? Just have a look at it, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise it, but I recognise the political content of the document, but I didn't see it before a couple of days ago, though I knew of its existence, but I recognise its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is that document?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a document confirming that already at the end of April and the beginning of May there was a possibility, without the violation of the vital interests of Serbia and Yugoslavia, the war with NATO to be ended and the continued suffering of our people to be brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When is it dated?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Lilic. I recognise his signature. I don't know Mr. Zoran Lilic, but I know from Mr. Vuk Draskovic, who spoke with Mr. Lilic several times about peace offers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To whom is the published letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You may have already said this, but when did you first see this letter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you referred to the contents or similar contents as is contained in this letter in your statement to the ICTY before you saw this document in its published form; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do have copies of this particular appendix which may be marked as exhibits in these proceedings. The witness has now recognised it and testified about it. Since we don't have copies of the book, I wonder whether I might be able to tender both the original copies of Appendix 4 and an English translation at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that this witness has no idea about -- as to whether Appendix 2 is a photocopy or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I didn't ask that question, but, Your Honour, my understanding is that Exhibit 2 is a photocopy of -- let me double-check because I didn't personally make the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask this: On page 160, there's a date in the first part of the letter which is written 23rd of July, 1998. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the last page is 164. There once again we have the date, 23rd of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To my eye, the letters themselves look different. Could you clarify that matter? Especially the number 7 is different, and 9 is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't focus on that particular aspect over the brief adjournment we had. Perhaps if you will allow me the opportunity to find out exactly whether this was photocopied or whether it's simply a copy of it, I will undertake to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, during the course of your cross-examination, the accused produced a document purporting to show your registration in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. capacity as a sympathiser with the New Democracy Party. Do you recall being shown that document?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: He went on to suggest in cross-examination that you were not a member or did not hold any specific function with that political party. Do you recall that aspect of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you familiar with the Bertelsmann Wissenschaftsstung system?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for interfering, but I can offer written evidence that I was an advisor of the president of New Democracy. Even the Prosecution doesn't have this document because I didn't consider all that to be necessary, and I do indeed apologise. But there is absolute direct evidence of that. I simply didn't know that I needed to prove to the Prosecution what is common knowledge in Belgrade. I'm sorry for the interfering.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No need. I'm going to ask -- I'm going to show you some documentation at this point. Sir, what is the Bertelsmann Wissenschaftsstung system? What kind of an organisation is that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what we call an NGO, a non-governmental organisation, a powerful NGO engaged in investigating peace settlements in various parts of the world. It is linked to the German government, and the director of the research project is Mr. Janning, who was an advisor, at that time at least, in the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you ever attend any of the conferences of that organisation, that NGO, as a representative of the New Democracy Party?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times, but as a representative of the ruling coalition. And I also did some writing for that foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, for example, sir, did you attend a conference of the Bertelsmann Wissenschaftsstung in Rhodes in September of 1996?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when I first brought an original copy of the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement, which was given to me by the ruling authorities in Serbia, and it was the first time to be taken abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you attend any further conferences of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attended several more, which were also attended by representatives of the Socialist Party of Serbia on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a series of documents I now wish to show to the witness, if I may. I have the originals and copies. First of all, perhaps we can -- in order to save time, just put the whole bundle in at once to everyone, and then I'll quickly refer to all of them rather than do them piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, here are some originals to go to the registrar, please, Mr. Usher. I intend to deal with these documents in the order that they are being handed out. And for the sake of convenience, perhaps the bundle might get an exhibit number, if Your Honours so choose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And for the record, the bundle that I'm handing are six separate documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, I'm showing you the first document which has a list of participants with the heading of "The Albanian Question in the Balkans in Rhodes September 5th through 6th of 1996." Do you see that document, the front page? Sorry. I'm just asking you to look at the front page now. Mr. Tanic, the question is: Do you see the page --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- list of participants, "The Albanian Question of the Balkans in Rhodes September 5th and 6th, 1996?" I don't have a response from you, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Looking at the second page following that, there's a number of people listed as having been participants in that -- at that conference, and on the second page, under number K0224112, your name appears fourth from the bottom. Do you see that? On the English version.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you are described there as the conciliarly to the president and secretary for international relations of New Democracy in Belgrade. Was that your function when you attended that particular conference?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can also provide my own documents; my party booklet, my card, party card.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not asking for that. I'm simply asking whether you recognise your name and described title as a participant at that conference. You're nodding your head, being yes?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very quickly, sir, look at the next document, list of participants in Munich, 21st to 22nd of January 1997, the same organisation. Front page, third name from the bottom, is that your name and your affiliation to New Democracy Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply can't find the page. I do apologise. Is it -- does it refer to Rhodes or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right, quite. I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next document titled List of Participants, Strategies and Options for Kosovo in Athens June 4th and 5th 1997. That's the title page. Over the page, your name, third from the bottom -- fourth from the bottom. And again your affiliation with New Democracy Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Next document. List of Participants, Strategies and Options for Kosovo in Halki, September 7th through 10th 1997. Next page, your name fourth from the bottom, New Democracy, Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And quickly, next document, again List of Participants, Strategies and Options for Kosovo, Thessaloniki, April 20th and 21st 1998. Your name, two pages down, looks to be about sixth from the bottom. Again New Democracy, Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- Balkans Security Risks and Implications for the European Union, again in Halki, September 7th through 9th 1998, and your name, second page, second from the bottom, again New Democracy, Belgrade? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a press conference on the 15th of September, 1994, wherein you were described in that press release that you were now a -- or words to the effect that you were now an advisor to the president of the New Democracy Party, responsible for international questions?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you, sir, first of all -- excuse me just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have copies of a press release dated the 16th of September 1994, both in its Cyrillic text, showing its source, then the second page is an enlarged copy of the article to which I'm referring, and the third page is an English translation of that article. If I might tender that as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, do you recognise this as being a photocopy of what appears to be a publication known as Politika, dated the 16th of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is Politika, the official organ of the Republic of Serbia. That is subject to censorship, therefore, only data that are correct can be published. And I do recognise this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, there's no need to give additional information. I'm asking you, first of all, do you recognise this as being -- and you've answered that. Now, I'd like you to turn your attention to the bottom third --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- bottom quarter, as it were. There seems to be an article which has as a headline, "New Democracy Press Conference." Do you see that article on the bottom quarter, right-hand corner of the page?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if you'll turn the page, please, in the bundle, there appears to be an enlargement of that particular article.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And does this article describe you as having recently resigned from the office of the vice-president and having left the Civic Alliance of Serbia and becoming a member of the New Democracy Party?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Does it go on to describe what your position would be with respect to the New Democracy Party? Was something announced there? Just look at that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I've looked at it. It does --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. What does it say --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- publish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- your job would be and what you would soon do, according to the press release from the party?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is said that my job would be advisor to president of New Democracy for international affairs and a member of the Executive Board of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few other questions, if I may, sir. Because time is of the essence, if possible if you could respond to my questions -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might we have an exhibit number before I move on in my haste.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Wherever possible, sir, just short succinct answers would be good. Have you maintained contact with Mr. Mihajlovic since you became a witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you ever tell Mihajlovic that you would be giving evidence at this trial?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we did discuss the problems linked to this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, just confining your answers, if possible, to yes or no, was the figure of the Albanian population in Kosovo being less than a million ever discussed in parliament or within the circles where you moved, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mentioned in private conversations by officials, in parliament -- in parliament, as far as I know, it was not, but I wasn't fully aware of what was happening in parliament, and I apologise for not being able to provide a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you aware whether it was ever discussed as anybody's official policy?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In no parliament was the problem of Kosovo ever discussed in that way or from the standpoint of investigating any other problems either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, has anyone ever suggested to you that you were kidnapped by anyone other than the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The results of the investigation showed officially that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And have you pursued any legal remedy or civil redress for this kidnapping from any source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the Minister of the Interior, Mihajlovic, and the heads of the State Security Service that the persons who perpetrated the kidnapping, after they were identified through an official investigation, that they should be arrested and charged. I personally did not undertake any steps because I do not have the conditions to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you complained and you sought that something be done about that fact, is that correct, through official channels?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the names that the investigation came up with, the people who had kidnapped me and my wife and tortured me, and everything else that I reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I just have one final matter, Your Honour. I understand there was a previous document that was tendered for which there was no translation, and I believe that we now -- this was supposedly -- this was during the course of Milosevic's cross-examination last day. He tried to tender this particular document. We now have a translation available, and perhaps this would be an appropriate time to introduce that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, I believe I've come to the end of my re-examination of this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Give that an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Defence Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I ask some questions, could he be given an English version of his statement, because I notice there are some discrepancies between the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No usher. May I approach the witness to -- oh, there he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'd like to ask a few questions regarding your written statements. It's on page 10 of your statements, English version. On the last part of third paragraph, you mention that: "Mr. Milosevic stated that there will be no negotiations, that he would prove there were less than 1 million Albanians, that war was nothing, and that there would be ethnic cleansing." I'd like to ask the -- ask about the final sentence about ethnic cleansing. Is that the exact words that Mr. Milosevic had said at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the words that Mr. Milosevic used, and other words too, that we would throw them out, who weren't -- I can't repeat all the words that were said, because quite simply ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in other parts of your statement, you said it is your conclusion, your speculations. Let's turn to page 20, third paragraph. At the last part, you said: "I concluded that Milosevic had a policy of killing Kosovo Albanian civilians." Oh, there might be a little difference, but -- so you are maintaining that Mr. Milosevic said to throw out the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do claim that, but everything that I need to prove and everything that cannot be proved I have taken upon myself personally. I think that was obvious throughout my testimony. But, yes, I do claim that Mr. Milosevic said that. There were statements to that effect earlier on, with respect to Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's go back to page 10 and at the next paragraph, you said that Mr. Martin Lutz asked you to set up a meeting with Mrs. Mira Markovic, and in the middle of the paragraph, you said that you organised the meeting in the spring of 1997. How did you organise that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After looking through my documents, I established that this was in fact in 1996, a year earlier. In the spring of 1996. I organised it on the basis of the fact that, as members of the ruling coalition, we had the right to inform each other, one another, and to have talks, and Mr. Lutz asked for assistance in a meeting with Mrs. Markovic, who is an influential political functionary, and that's how the meeting came to be organised, quite simply. Via the official channels of communication between the three ruling coalition parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your party that organised the meeting, rather than you in person?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I organised it through the channels of official communication. I wasn't a friend of Mrs. Markovic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Turn to page 11 then. In the third paragraph, you pointed out some difference between two autonomies. I'll read it. "However, after concluding this agreement with Holbrooke, Milosevic sent Serb negotiators to Kosovo 13 times to discuss the autonomy of the province and not of the Kosovo Albanians, thus acting completely opposite to a political solution." What is the difference between the autonomy of the province and that of people?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference lies in the fact that the autonomy of the people, in this case the Albanians, incorporates the rights to their specific national political identity within the frameworks of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And the autonomy for the whole province would imply that, for example, 1.000 members of the Roma people or 100 Egyptians, for example, living in Kosovo should be equated with the 1.2 million, approximately, of Albanians. So that is the difference and that is the difference that was always insisted upon so precision was always made whether what was referred to was the autonomy of the province or the autonomy of the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then page 12, at the third paragraph, you said that the Italian ambassador in Belgrade asked you to convey to Mr. Milosevic their willingness to assist in eliminating the KLA. Why did the Italians choose you to convey their willingness? In what capacity did you have contact with them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two reasons: One is that I had personally good contacts with the Italian political establishment and the ambassador in question; and the second reason was that my party was considered to be the most liberal within the frameworks of the ruling coalition. And so usually all the messages that were to be conveyed and prepared -- and to prepare a more liberal solution usually went via our party, my party. And I, as the advisor of the president, was present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My last question is that, at page 25, the third paragraph: "Milosevic knew that there would be a NATO attack if he continued ethnic cleansing of the Kosovo Albanians or other violent operations in Kosovo. In the summer of 1998, I was informed of this by my Western contacts." Could you clarify, what you mean by these "Western contacts"?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Italian, British, German diplomacy. The diplomacies of those countries, not the intelligence services, the diplomacies of those countries, to send out a warning that the problem should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in connection with this question, may I be allowed, with regard to the question that Mr. Kwon asked, may I ask a question myself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, one question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to divide it up into two or three. What kind of ethnic cleansing of Albanians and, generally speaking, the suffering of the Albanians existed before the war began?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean with the Albanians or with the NATO pact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the NATO pact aggression against Yugoslavia began. That's what I'm asking about. What kind of mass suffering of Albanians were these?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Cicavica mountain, on the Kosovo side of Mount Kopaonik, at Laba, six weeks after the Serb forces had regularly taken control of Junik and that the international community agreed to, six weeks after that, ethnic cleansing was continued via Cicavica mountain and on the Kosovo side of Kopaonik and Labo. That is just one example. And the Serb victims, these continued among the police force and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking about the event in Racak? Do you believe that to be some kind of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I quoted just one example. To quote other examples would take up too much time. And I too would like to say something. As His Honour Judge May said this morning, he said I would be allowed to say a few words at the end this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you the following: Do you consider that the so-called massacre, as Walker referred to it, in Racak was in fact that ethnic cleansing of Albanians before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's a matter which we're going to have to deal with. We're going to have to consider that. Now, is there any other question that you want to ask arising from what Judge Kwon said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanians -- before the NATO aggression started, how many Albanians were killed in Kosovo by, as you claim, the forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia? How many Albanians at all died in Kosovo before the war began?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- I'm not -- it wasn't a question of killing but that they were expelled from their homes, their passports were torn up, all these things. So not just killings. They were expelled from their houses, their ID papers and passports were torn up to destroy their identity and similar things. Of course, the Serb forces did not fully fulfil your wishes, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, that is to say until the beginning of the war, there was the Verification Mission present in Kosovo, the OSCE one? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you called their results false. Now, if you recognise them now, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Verification Mission and their presence in Kosovo. And as you know very well, there is no ethnic cleansing and everything that you're claiming there. There were 1.300 verifiers there.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in their reports and in your talks to Yeltsin and other statesmen, massacres were always mentioned and expulsions as well. They weren't always killings. At the Cicavica plant in the Kosovo part of Kopaonik and after Junik was returned, that was what triggered off this wave of refugees to Albania, and Albania refugees and in Montenegro. So the Serb forces did not carry out all your orders and that serves to their honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, that all of the foreign politicians so far said that Racak was in fact what triggered off the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to continue this. That's a comment which you make frequently, and it's of no help putting it again. The registrar wishes to make a correction about Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The letter from the Ministry of Internal Affairs is actually D12, and the statement by New Democracy dated 14 May 2002 is D13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tanic, our procedures do not allow for statements by witnesses. I understand that there are some documents which you wish to hand over. The way to do that is to give them to the Prosecution. You could now speak to the Prosecution since your evidence is over. Give them to the Prosecution, and they can then deal with them and put them in front of the Court as need be. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let's get the -- I thought the witness was going to be in. We've been a very long time during this break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought the witness was going to be in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break, I have been supplied with a bunch of documents from the last witness. As you know, once a witness leaves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I said he was to give them to you. Mr. Ryneveld, what do you want to do with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will present these documents to the Court in due course. In the interim and in fairness, I have on the ELMO at the moment, subject to the Court's permission, three photographs which the Court ought see at this particular point since this witness's -- since the previous witness's evidence has been questioned. They're photographs that show him in the company of Mr. Milosevic, in the company of Mr. Mihajlovic, and in the company of Mr. Milutinovic. In just one second, I've shown them both to the amici and to the accused. The issue of his credibility is for this Court, but I would submit that it's important that it be shown immediately that some of the things that he's been testifying to are in fact borne out in documentary fashion. That is in addition to documents we will be presenting in due course by leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen the documents, the photographs. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I first say something with respect to those photographs, as the other side mentioned them, brought them up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that photograph, for example, where you can see the reception of the Novo Demokratija delegation, that particular photograph showing the reception indicates what I said, that it was a delegation that numbered numerous people. And as you can see, Mr. Tanic was escorting this delegation, which is borne out by his position in the photograph. And I suppose they used him to bring in some books or pictures or something else that they needed. So there's no question of a meeting between himself, myself, and Mihajlovic, but it was a mass reception of the delegation of the Novo Demokratija Party. And at any rate, we heard the opposite side presenting a series of evidence here that proves nothing except that he was an employee of the Novo Demokratija Party in the capacity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can present evidence on it in due course. Meanwhile, we've seen the photographs, we will have them exhibited. Next Prosecution exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have an answer, a response to the question asked by Mr. Robinson, and I wasn't able to answer him because I did not have knowledge of the legal rules, but in the break, I have procured the answer, the exact answer to his question. According to the district court procedure and rules, I'm talking about Belgrade, Article 199, paragraph 3 says that if somebody is convicted in a trial, according to legal proceedings, and receives a prison sentence of up to one year, this material is kept for a period of ten years. All the papers are kept for a period of ten years, after which they are destroyed. But a permanent record is kept of them for the purposes of the court. So it is completely uncontestable what it says in the attestation given by the district court which I supplied in the original. It is quite clear that Mr. Tanic was found guilty for the crime of robbery and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right. If you have that, then let me move on to my next objection, and that has to do with the forthcoming witness, Dr. Eric Baccard. What I want to say is this: You have assumed the position with respect to 38 registers, and I see that there is an enormous amount of physical work done here by the employees of the Tribunal, bringing in piles of files and binders, and you concluded that these 38 binders were a component part of his report. So in that sense, I have an objection to make with respect to your own rules and regulations, because I consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find out what the binders are here for from the Prosecution and then we can hear any objections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. May I just explain what I wanted to say, what I wanted to make as an objection? Those 38 binders, they are heavy binders, were sent to me in the English language, the English version, and I think that not even an average literate English man, with respect to the professional terminology used, is not able to read through all that material. And according to your own Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you were duty-bound to supply me with them in the Serbian language because an expert report and finding must be also looked into by my professional associates and not by me alone. And that is why I consider that the cross-examination of this witness can only refer to his report per se, whereas all the other 38 binders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is the only material but for some reason, which we haven't yet been enlightened, other documents have been brought in. Let's hear what they're here for and then we can go further from there. But at the moment we know no more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was about to do that. I might say, Your Honour, there have -- you will recall a discussion with the Prosecution some time ago in open court at which time Mr. Nice outlined the fact that there were a number of binders by municipality that would be of assistance to the Court. The Court made a ruling with respect to what could and could not be contained in those binders, and those binders have now been edited in accordance with the Chamber's ruling as given by Judge Robinson on behalf of the Chamber. These are for the various 12 what have been referred to as killing sites, and they contain a compendium of the material that has been viewed by the Court, at least with respect to -- I believe the Court looked at one sample municipality binder, Bela Crkva. These are now the balance of the binders for the additional municipalities. It made sense, in our respectful submission, that these binders be tendered at this particular time, (a), because we said we would do that as quickly as possible and people have been feverishly working to get this done, and (b), because it relates to the evidence of our expert witness, Dr. Eric Baccard. Dr. Baccard is the forensic pathologist who reviewed all of the various exhumation and pathology reports. He was the supervisor of the pathologists, the various teams who conducted all of the autopsies for these various municipalities. His report was prepared and has been tendered. A copy of all this documentation was given to the accused in black and white prior to the commencement of the trial. He's had this since February. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that he can follow this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- this is all material which has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All that has happened is that this documentation has been collected and put into binders relating to each place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct. For ease of reference, municipality by municipality, as the Court indicated its preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It contains no new material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And indeed we did rule, not very long ago, that we would admit these binders for ease of reference. Now, just dealing with Dr. Baccard, the idea, presumably, is that he will refer to his own reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct. But in his report, and just so that the Court, again for ease of reference, this is a potentially tedious and lengthy process. In order to do this as quickly and efficiently and as logical as possible, it was my suggestion that we put the binders in, have them marked as exhibits, dealing with Dr. Baccard, and supply the Court with an index for each site in his report to the tab numbers in the municipal site. In other words, that is the source material for his report. I intend to deal with Dr. Baccard only with respect to his report, and the source material will be referenced to the Court in case the court wants to refer to the actual reports by tab number. For example, if we deal with, say, Bela Crkva site, we have an index for Bela Crkva. It's two binders, and it deals at tab 8 with the British forensic team exhumation report. That goes site by site, how many binders, and exactly what tab number refers to references in Dr. Baccard's report and its table of contents. That, we thought was the most efficient way to deal with it. Unless the Court has a preference for me to do it piecemeal and one by one. We'll be here quite awhile if I have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we have the position fully, all this material has been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have arranged it in this way and have been allowed to do so so that not only the Trial Chamber but the parties can find their way around the material. The witness will refer to his reports; is this right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But only if there is a requirement to look at some original which is referred to in the report will it be necessary to look at these binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. It may be that those binders will not have to be touched during the course of my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, but it may be that we have an understanding of this problem. It's the translation of the material within those binders that has been the problem for the accused. The disclosure has been in the English language. I know for our part that Mr. Tapuskovic has had to have the binders translated to him by his assistant from the English language to the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's all been disclosed, as I understand it. These binders contain nothing new. That's the crucial point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not in the B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the debate. The binders contain nothing new; they merely contain documents which have been disclosed before. The witness will give evidence from his report, and can be cross-examined about it. If some issue arises about nondisclosure in B/C/S, then we'll listen to it at the time, but for the moment, we will go on, and we'll deal with the report. The binders are a complete side issue at the moment. Yes. Let's call the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I state something further, please, another piece of information? The binders or, rather, the documents were given in colour only on Friday. For professionals to examine these, it makes a difference whether the photographs are in black and white or in colour, and when they were supplied, because professionals are not able to examine them, black and white differs from colour. Now, as none of these binders have been provided in the Serbian language and in view of the fact that on Friday, that is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop. There is a confusion here. The binders are not new material. They are old material which has been arranged in a different way for the convenience of all, including your side, so that when you come to a particular site, you will have all the evidence about it. Now, let us not continue this argument. You've had, I suspect, a long time to prepare for it. Now we'll have -- I think we don't have a number for those last photographs. We'll have a number for them and then we'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The three photographs will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 155.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. May I say what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. You've made your point. Let us call the witness. We have now wasted 20 minutes and more with argument. Let us call the witness, and if there are difficulties about it and examination of him, we'll hear you in due course, but let's hear his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I call Dr. Eric Baccard. And while we're awaiting his arrival, I might just add that Dr. Baccard's report has also been disclosed in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you take the declaration, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, I understand, sir, that you are the chief forensic pathologist for the ICTY in Kosovo, and you've been acting as a consultant to the ICTY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You've been a medical doctor since 1981?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You received your speciality in pathology in 1985?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I received that in 1985, but I had begun it much earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. You had some subspecialties as well, and in 1980, you received a speciality in evaluation of bodily damage; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we call the evaluation of bodily damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And you've also completed a speciality in forensic criminalistics, which includes such things as DNA, the forensic criminal aspects of pathology?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. The diploma was issued in Paris and is known as a diploma in criminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, you also received your diploma in wound ballistics in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. I think that must -- it must have been that year. Yes, it was a diploma from the faculty of medicine of Marseilles, and I was in the top of my class.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Baccard, I understand that as part of your report, you have submitted your curriculum vitae at page 80 of your 154-page report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, sir, so that the Court understands some background as well, you are not only a forensic pathologist but a wound ballistics expert for France; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. I am an expert in forensic medicine, and an expert as well for the Cour de Cassation, the only expert at that court in France, authorised by that court as a forensic pathologist with specialisation in ballistics, ballistic wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Over the years since you developed your expertise, are you able to estimate how many written expert reports you may have submitted to various courts in your home country of France?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to give you an exact figure. I think it must be several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, have you been permitted by the courts -- qualified as an expert and allowed to express opinions in oral testimony in the courts of France concerning your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. I am on the list of experts for the appeals court of Grenoble and, as I said, I am on the national list of experts with authorisation or qualification from the Cour de Cassation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, turning to your work history with respect to matters of the Balkans conflict, I understand that you were the chief forensic pathologist for the ICTY in Kosovo in March of 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I worked also with the Office of the Prosecutor in 1999 in Visoko in Bosnia and then in Zagreb in Croatia as a forensic pathologist. In March of 2000 that I took over the direction of the Orahovac morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you say you took over the direction of the Orahovac morgue, were you in charge of a number of forensic pathologists who were conducting the autopsies? Were you the chief pathologist?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I talk about being in charge, I'm talking about scientific responsibility, and as such, my responsibilities were also myself to carry out, to perform autopsies and also to personally supervise the work carried out by my various foreign colleagues who came to the ICTY morgue in Orahovac in 2000, as they would come one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, I take it then during the course of your duties you reviewed a number of reports prepared by these different international teams of pathologists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Not only did I supervise the performance of the autopsies in 2000 in Orahovac, but I also reread all of the reports that have been drafted by my colleagues during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dealing very briefly with the methodology that you used in compiling your report, are you able to give the Court an indication as to how many sites and subsites there may have been into which you have, shall we say, divided your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. The sites are listed in my report on page 9. These are the sites at Bela Crkva, Djakovica, the Milos Gilic Street incident, Djakovica the incident on Ymer Grezda Street, in Dubrava in the Dubrava prison, in Izbica, in Kotlina, in Krusha e Vogel, in Padalishte, in Racak, in Stagovo, Studime e Eperme, in Suva Reka and Vata.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, in saying that there were some 11 main sites of which one had four subsites, in your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, is it my understanding that all of the bodies, wherever they were found, would have been transported to the mortuaries in Orahovac where you were working, apart from the ones that were in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: In referring to the year -- the mission for 2000, yes. For 1999, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. In 1999, where were they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The bodies were autopsied in morgues, either official morgues or improvised ones, and carried out by the various international pathologist teams and the location of the autopsies is indicated for each site in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, perhaps we can just give the Court a thumbnail sketch as to how it is that you went about preparing your report. I take it that you received individual pathology reports from the various international teams that had performed autopsies from various sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The first task that I had to carry out was to identify what the sources of information in terms of forensic medicine existed to which I could refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: That first step thus allowed us to bring out several documents on which I could base my analysis. I am referring now to the autopsy reports but also to the anthropological expertise reports, the examination reports on crime sites -- at crime sites, the albums of photographs and both photographs that were taken during the autopsies and/or photographs taken on site, and sometimes as well there was testimony of witnesses. In one specific case, which is the case of Izbica, in addition to the documents previously listed, I worked from a copy of the video cassette and photographs which had been extracted from that video cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, sir, these reports that you had available to you were complete reports with photographs, et cetera, and you're aware that they have now been placed into various binders by site; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: The reports were, in fact, reports that were more or less complete because each international team had its own way of working, and the reports were accompanied with the photographs, of course. And I know that the reports were put into binders on which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, the reference to certain reports are contained in your report, and they refer to the individual reports prepared by other forensic teams which you examined, reviewed, and commented upon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you carried out, as I understand it, a rather exhaustive review of all of these reports. That took you approximately six months or so?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: I think that we could say that it was an average of about six months. Six months of work that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where you found errors or discrepancies or issues that you did not agree with or were not supported in your review, did you make a note of those observations in your report to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. Also when I spoke about the first stage of the methodology that was used, that is to -- to go through the various documents I had available to me, that stage was then followed by another one which was to read the reports prepared by my colleagues and to compare them with the other reports that had been made by crime scene technicians and to compare them to the photographs that were taken at the time of the autopsies and on the sites. In the annex of this report, there are several documents which point out to discrepancies I might have -- that I sometimes noted during the comparative study.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So where you found discrepancies between the report and your own observations, you would have made a note of them in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the contradictions are pointed out in the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mention that there was one somewhat unusual site in the sense that the bodies had not been autopsied themselves, I take it. Is that correct? I'm referring, of course, to Izbica.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did that site differ from the other sites?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD
